topic: Loss aversion: why losses feel bigger than gains (and who disagrees)
title: Does Losing Really Hurt More Than Winning?
voiceover: Why does losing feel worse than winning feels good? In 1979, Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky proposed prospect theory. One key idea is loss aversion: losses loom larger than equivalent gains. In 1992, Tversky and Kahneman estimated a loss-aversion coefficient of about 2.25. Roughly speaking, that means a loss counts about twice as much as a gain of the same size. But the idea is contested. In 2018, David Gal and Derek Rucker reviewed the evidence and concluded that losses, on balance, are not more impactful than gains. They argue the impact of losses versus gains depends on context. So treat 'losses hurt twice as much' as a debated rule of thumb, not a law. When you hear it, ask: in which situation, and compared with what? Tomorrow: do unskilled people really think they're geniuses?

description: Do losses really hurt about twice as much as equal gains? That's the classic prospect-theory idea, but a 2018 review argued the evidence doesn't support it as a general rule. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Kahneman, D., & Tversky, A. (1979). Prospect theory: An analysis of decision under risk. Econometrica, 47(2), 263-291. Source: Gal, D., & Rucker, D. D. (2018). The loss of loss aversion: Will it loom larger than its gain?. Journal of Consumer Psychology, 28(3), 497-516.
accuracy_note: CONTESTED. 'About twice' reflects a model parameter (2.25) fitted to certain gambling choices (Tversky & Kahneman 1992). Gal & Rucker (2018) argue evidence does not support losses being more impactful on balance and that context matters; defenders of loss aversion disagree. Video presents it as a debated rule of thumb.
